BEETHOVEN TRIAL EDITION LICENSE AGREEMENT

Licensed software, by approval. Beethoven is licensed, not sold: you receive a license to use it under the Trial Edition License Agreement below and the privacy statement, accepted once in a signing dialog on the extension's own setup page. The Trial Edition is free for approved institutional accounts during the evaluation period; a paid Full Edition, if offered, is a separate agreement. 1. WHAT BEETHOVEN IS

"Beethoven" means the browser extension of that name (the "Extension"), the scripts and programs that your institution's lab keeps in one shared copy on your institution's cluster, which the Extension points your computing account at, or that an earlier version of the Extension installed in your own computing account (either way, the "Framework"), the recipe for the container image the Framework runs, its documentation, and updates Licensor provides. The Extension starts, watches and stops a job in your own cluster account through your institution's Open OnDemand portal, in a browser session signed in to there, by you or, with the account name and password you give it, by the Extension (section 5(b)(i)); the job runs Claude Code, Anthropic's program, which you have signed in to yourself, and makes that session visible to you at claude.ai and in the Claude app through Anthropic's Remote Control feature. "Trial Edition" means the edition this agreement covers: free of charge during the evaluation period, for persons whose institutional account Licensor has approved. "Full Edition" means the paid edition, if Licensor offers one, governed by the separate Beethoven Full Edition License Agreement, which you accept only if you choose that edition. "Your portal" means your institution's Open OnDemand portal, and "your account name" means the name of your account on your institution's cluster as the cluster confirms it when you or the Extension signs in: the name your portal's dashboard shows for that session. It is the only identifier of you that Beethoven uses to know who you are (the Extension also names its own installation with a random number, section 3(e)); an account name you type to sign in (section 5(b)(i)) is used only to sign in. "Named Dependencies" are the outside parties and conditions listed in section 7.

3. APPROVAL AND WITHDRAWAL

(a) The Trial Edition is available only to persons whose institutional account Licensor has approved for it. Approval is requested on the request page at https://openspineconsortium.com/beethoven/request.html, with your account name and the Google account at which you are to receive the invitation to the Extension's private listing, and may be refused or withdrawn at any time, with or without reason. Licensor may approve an account for membership of its lab only; such an approval does not cover Beethoven. There is no key and no password of Licensor's: your own sign-in to your institution's cluster identifies you. After you have accepted this agreement, and only once your cluster has accepted your sign-in to your portal, the Extension asks Licensor's access service whether your account name is approved: when you first sign in after accepting it, about once a day while it is in use, and again when you open its panel after a day has passed or after a no; and it starts a worker only while the answer is yes. A copy of Beethoven used from an account that is not approved does not start a worker; its panel offers a link to ask for access instead.

(b) Your approval is for you and the institutional account it names alone. Do not use Beethoven from an account that is not yours, and do not arrange for anyone else to use it under your approval. Sharing your copy of Beethoven, your installation of it or your account with anyone else is a breach of this agreement.

(c) No payment is taken for the Trial Edition, nothing converts automatically into a paid license, and no charge follows its end. Beethoven contains the code that asks for and enforces approval; you may not disable, remove or work around it.

(d) Licensor may withdraw an approval that has been misused (including one shared with anyone else or used from an installation other than yours), given in error or obtained by misrepresentation, or for any other reason. Once your approval is withdrawn, the Extension stops starting workers at its next check and tells you so. Beethoven also checks its own version against a signed list of withdrawn versions; a withdrawn version stops sending commands and tells you to update.

(e) One installation. Your approval covers one installation of the Extension: one browser profile on one computer. The Extension makes a random installation identifier for itself the first time it needs one (when you accept this agreement), from the browser's random number generator; it is not taken or derived from your computer, its hardware or anything else about you, and it is removed when you uninstall the Extension, so a reinstallation is a new installation. The first installation that asks about your approved account is bound to it. An approval check from any other installation (another computer, another browser profile or a reinstallation) is refused, and the Extension says so, until Licensor moves your approval to that installation; ask your lab lead, or write to the notice address on the support page. Likewise, an installation bound to one approved account serves that account only: a check from it for any other account is refused, and the Extension says so, until Licensor releases it. Licensor may refuse every check from a version of the Extension that sends no installation identifier; the current version is on the private listing.

Beethoven works with accounts and systems that are yours or your institution's, not Licensor's. You represent that you are the sole holder of, and authorised to use, each account Beethoven touches, and you agree to use Beethoven only in compliance with each of the following, as amended from time to time:

(b) Anthropic's Consumer Terms of Service, Usage Policy and the Claude Code terms, including the terms for Remote Control, for your Claude account: one person, one account; no sharing of credentials; no use of another person's account;

5. WHAT BEETHOVEN DOES WITH YOUR CREDENTIALS AND YOUR WORK

This section describes the software as shipped, so that you can hold Licensor to it.

(a) Claude. Beethoven never reads, stores, copies, prints or relays a Claude credential. You sign in to Claude Code yourself, through Anthropic's own flow, once, in a terminal on a compute node of your own cluster account. The Extension starts that terminal for you, in the same command that starts your worker, through your portal's shell, opens Anthropic's sign-in page in a new tab, shows you one box, and closes that tab once Claude Code reports you are signed in, unless the tab has loaded another page since you pasted the code; you sign in on Anthropic's page and paste the one-time code it shows into that box. The Extension types the code once into that terminal and keeps no copy of it: it is not stored, not written to the audit log and not sent to Licensor or anyone else, and the Extension never reads Anthropic's page or your clipboard to obtain it. Claude Code makes its credential from the code and keeps it in its own folder in your cluster account; the Framework only starts Claude Code where that credential already is, and Beethoven reads Claude Code's own report of whether it is signed in, with the account and plan that report names, nothing more. You use one Claude account, your own. You answer Claude Code's one-time question about Remote Control yourself, with the box you tick in the Extension's panel before your first worker starts; the Framework records that answer in one file in your cluster account when you press Connect, and your worker gives it to Claude Code when Claude Code asks. Trust for the worker's own folder is recorded in Claude Code's settings by the Framework when a worker starts. Beethoven gives Claude Code no answer you have not given.

(b) Your sign-in to your cluster. The Extension reaches your cluster in one way: through your institution's Open OnDemand portal, which may need your institution's VPN (at Wayne State, GlobalProtect), in a browser session signed in to there. It signs in to your portal for you with the account name and password you give it, or uses the sign-in you make yourself in your browser's own sign-in box, as (i) says. It never signs in to Claude for you (see (a)). Versions 12.0.0 to 15.0.0 of the Extension also offered a direct way over ssh, through a helper program (the "Bridge") installed on your computer, a sign-in sheet of the Extension's own and a key kept in your browser; this version has no Bridge, no ssh connection of its own and no such key, and (ii) says what it leaves alone. The sign-in sheet of (i) is not that way: it signs in to your portal only, over the same connection as everything else the Extension does there, which still needs your institution's VPN where it requires one, and it asks for no verification code.

(i) Your portal. The Extension makes its requests to your institution's Open OnDemand portal, on that one website only, from its own background and without a portal tab where your browser allows it, with the sign-in your browser holds for that website. It never reads that sign-in and never touches a multi-factor step. When the portal asks for a sign-in, the Extension signs in for you with the password you give it, or you sign in yourself in your browser's own sign-in box.

The Extension's own sign-in. Where your browser lets the Extension answer a website's request for a sign-in, as Chrome does, it asks for your account name and your cluster password on its own sign-in sheet, in its panel, whenever your portal wants a sign-in. By typing them there and pressing "Sign in" you ask the Extension to sign in to your portal for you with them, and agree that it may. It answers, through your browser and not with a page script, only the portal's request for a sign-in that its own background reading of your portal's dashboard page receives, at most once each time it checks whether you are signed in, and only when that request comes from your one portal website itself, not from a proxy, asks for the portal's plain ("Basic") sign-in and, once a password the Extension gave has worked, in this browser session or, for the saved password, at any time since it was saved, names the same sign-in realm as that one; a sign-in in your browser's own box records no realm, and Forget, Disconnect and a change of portal remove the one on record. It never answers such a request from one of your browser tabs, which gets your browser's own sign-in box, nor from a proxy, another website or another realm, nor for the checks that ask whether your portal answers, which carry no sign-in. Of your own portal tabs' requests it keeps one mark only, and only while an answer it gave still waits for its outcome: that one of those tabs asked for a sign-in, or had a request answered by your portal without a refusal, meanwhile (see "One wrong password at most"); it keeps nothing about the tab or the request itself. It sends your password only to your portal, over the encrypted connection, as your browser's own box would; never to Licensor or anyone else. It never writes the password to a log, the audit log or the activity list, and keeps it only as the next paragraphs say. It never fills in a sign-in web page or your institution's identity provider, and never types a password into a shell (see the one-time step below). The account name you type is used only to sign in: the account name of section 1, which the approval check sends, is still the one your portal's dashboard shows.

One wrong password at most. The Extension sends a password your cluster turns down at most once. The first refusal stops every sign-in the Extension makes by itself, with a saved password or one you have just typed, until you type the password again on the sheet, and a saved password your cluster turned down is not tried again after a restart of the Extension or of your browser; the sheet then asks you to check the password before you try again. Where the Extension cannot tell whether a password it gave worked, because your browser closed, or the Extension updated or reloaded, before your cluster replied, or because one of your portal tabs asked for a sign-in or had a request answered while that answer waited (you may have signed in in your browser's own box, and your browser may have used that password for the Extension's request as well), it counts the try as neither a success nor a refusal and puts a saved password on hold: the Extension does not send it again until a password you type on the sheet works, or you save one again. Your browser also keeps its own copy of a password it is given (see below) and sends it again by itself: when your cluster turns that password down, your browser re-sends its cached copy once for each request already started with it before the first refusal comes back; the Extension then sends at most one; when the answered request is abandoned before your cluster replies, your browser may re-send that copy once. How many of these your cluster counts is not yet measured. Your institution may disable your account after a few wrong passwords, and getting it back may take days; a password you have just changed may not work everywhere yet. You accept that risk as a Known Risk (section 8).

Saving the password. Saving it is optional and off unless you tick the box "Remember it on this computer" on the sheet; the box is never ticked for you. Section 4(a) applies to that choice: where your institution says to type your password each time you need it, as Wayne State's password standard does, leave the box unticked. Unticked, the Extension keeps the password only in your browser's memory, for that one sign-in, and removes it afterwards, whether or not it worked, and at the latest two minutes after you pressed "Sign in". Ticked, the Extension has your computer make a passkey for it, unlocked with Windows Hello, Touch ID or your screen lock and named with your account name followed by "(grid)" (for example, "ab1234 (grid)"), and keeps the password in this browser profile, on this computer only, encrypted under a key that only that passkey releases. To use it you unlock it with the passkey, once each time you open your browser, when the Extension next needs your portal; what the passkey released stays in your browser's memory until the browser closes or the Extension updates or reloads, and the Extension then signs in with it when your portal asks, also while none of its pages is open. The passkey is kept by Windows Hello, your Mac's Passwords app (iCloud Keychain) or Chrome's password manager, not by the Extension; that store may keep it in your Google account or in iCloud and offer it on your other devices, but the saved password itself stays only in this browser profile. Someone who can use this browser profile while the saved password is unlocked, or who can unlock your passkey, could sign in to your portal with it, and so could the Extension's own code. Where your computer's passkey cannot lock a password, the Extension says so, uses the password for that one sign-in and from then on offers no box. "Forget", beside "Grid sign-in" in the Extension's Settings, deletes the saved password and everything the Extension keeps about it; Disconnect and changing to another portal do the same, and uninstalling the Extension removes it with the rest of its data. Forget may ask your passkey store to remove the passkey, but some stores keep it: your list of passkeys may still show it, and you can delete it there, after Forget. If a password you typed works while your saved one is turned down or on hold, the Extension forgets the saved one by itself, unless it can tell that the saved one is the same password, which it then keeps and uses again.

Your browser stays signed in. Once your cluster has accepted a password the Extension gave it, your browser keeps it in its memory, as it keeps one you type into its own box, and sends it to your portal from your own portal tabs as well, until the browser closes or you clear its browsing data with cookies; Forget and Disconnect do not end that.

Your browser's own sign-in box. "Use Chrome's sign-in box instead", on the sheet, opens the portal in a tab for you to sign in there, in your browser's own sign-in box or on the portal's own sign-in page; where the Extension cannot answer your portal's request for a sign-in, this is the only way. That includes a portal that sends you to your institution's own sign-in page instead of asking your browser for a password: the sheet may still appear there, but the Extension sends no password typed on it. The Extension never sees what you type in that tab, and closes it once you are signed in, while it is still on the portal. Your browser may offer to save what you type there; that offer, and where your browser keeps what it saves, are your browser's own, and section 4(a) applies to them too. Where your portal does not share its sign-in with the Extension, it keeps that tab behind your other tabs until the work in hand is done and then closes it, and for a later action opens the portal in a background tab and closes it again.

The one thing it reads about you from the portal is your account name, from the portal's own dashboard page. If your portal's shell asks for your cluster password, as it may for an account that has no key on the cluster, the Extension types nothing there, not even a password you gave it for the sign-in above, and offers a one-time step instead: it opens the portal's own terminal page in a tab, and you type your password there yourself; the Extension never sees it. Once you say you are in, or the page's title shows that your shell is up, the Extension types one line into that terminal (or leaves it on your clipboard for you to paste), which runs the Framework's login-setup step in your own account. That step makes a key in your cluster account, in its ~/.ssh folder, that opens your account only from the computer the terminal came from, which at your institution is its Open OnDemand server (it is a file in your own account, protected as your other files are, and hidden from Claude Code inside your worker; anyone who obtained it and could connect from that server could use it), and has ssh offer it when the portal's shell connects you, so that the shell need not ask for your password; it never reads, changes or prints a key you already have. The key stays in your cluster account: the Extension never sees it, keeps nothing about it in your browser and sends nothing about it to Licensor. The command "hpcworker login-setup --remove", run in a terminal on the cluster, removes it. This step has been tried only against the Licensor's mock portal, not yet on a real cluster by an account without a key.

(ii) What an earlier version may have left. If you used the direct way of versions 12.0.0 to 15.0.0 of the Extension on this computer, three things of it may remain, and this version uses none of them. The Bridge stays installed on your computer until you remove it: on Windows, from Windows' own list of installed apps, where it is called "Beethoven bridge"; on macOS and Linux, and for a Bridge installed from a zip file with Beethoven 14.0.0 or earlier, with the uninstaller placed beside it. This version holds no permission to start it, and your browser starts it for nothing. The line that version added to your account's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys file on your cluster stays until it is removed. This version deletes the key that line admitted from your browser, unread, on its first run after the update, so the line now admits nothing; it never let that key run anything but the Framework's gate, a fixed list of short commands, and this version never uses the line and never types a command for it. Your lab lead can remove the line for you, and the command "hpcworker browser-key remove", run in a terminal on your cluster, removes it; withdrawing your approval under section 3 does not. Where that version recorded that it had added such a line, the Extension's Settings say so once, with the date, and offer "Forget", which removes only that note from your browser and changes nothing on your cluster. A passkey you made to protect that key, the old passkey of versions 12.0.0 to 15.0.0, is kept by your system or your browser's password manager, not by the Extension; it is named with your account name alone, or "beethoven", this version never uses it, and you can delete it there. It is not the passkey of (i), named with your account name followed by "(grid)", which this version uses for a saved password: delete that one only after Forget.

(c) Your account name, as your cluster confirmed it, and the answer of the last approval check with its time are stored in the Extension's own storage in your browser. What the sign-in of (b)(i) keeps in your browser, and for how long, is listed in PRIVACY.md. Nothing about your approval is copied to your cluster account; the Framework has no key, password or account list of Licensor's.

(d) The Framework makes a random token for each job so that only your own browser session can reach your worker. It is kept in a file only you can read, is never shown, and never appears on a command line or in a job log.

(e) Where your work goes. Files the worker reads and every command's output are sent to Anthropic. While you are connected through claude.ai the transcript is also stored on Anthropic's servers. A personal plan is retained five years if model training is on and 30 days otherwise. No BAA covers a personal plan. FERPA records, IRB data and export-controlled technical data must not be in the working directory. Remote Control usage draws from your plan's shared limit. The Extension shows these sentences in short form, with the full text one click away, before your first worker starts, and a one-line reminder beside Connect each time you start one, and does not start a worker in a folder you have marked restricted.

(f) The Extension runs no code on claude.ai or any other Anthropic page and reads nothing from them. Its only page script runs on the one portal website you connect: where your portal does not share its sign-in with the Extension, to carry the Extension's requests there, and, during the one-time step in (b)(i), on the portal's terminal page, where it watches only the page's title and types only the one line described there. It opens an Anthropic page only in a new tab, as a bookmark would: the sign-in page during the sign-in described in (a), your worker's session page when a worker you started is ready (unless you turn that off) and when you choose "Open my session" or "New session", the connectors settings page if you choose the optional Google Drive step, and the plans page if you follow "See plans" on the welcome page; it closes the sign-in tab it opened once you are signed in, and it may bring forward a claude.ai tab it opened itself. Of an Anthropic tab it opened, it learns only that the tab has begun loading a page, which the browser tells it without the page's address or content. In the same way, the welcome page and the step that asks you to turn on your VPN link your institution's own pages about its computing accounts and its VPN; each opens in a new tab only when you choose it, and the Extension learns nothing of your visit.

(g) Of (a) to (f), only your account name in (c) is sent to Licensor, in the approval check that section 10 describes; nothing else is, and in particular not your cluster password or the account name you type to sign in. Section 10 describes the only things that may be.

7. NAMED DEPENDENCIES: THE OUTSIDE THINGS BEETHOVEN NEEDS

Beethoven works only while all of the following hold. None of them is within Licensor's control, and each is disclosed here, on the welcome page and where Beethoven is offered, so that you can decide with this in mind:

(a) your institution keeps your account, your access to its network (including any VPN it requires), its Open OnDemand portal with its shell, files and jobs features and, where used, its reverse proxy, and its computing systems; and its policies, firewalls, maintenance windows, queue rules and job limits allow what Beethoven does;

(b) Anthropic keeps offering Claude, Claude Code, its sign-in flow, the subscription plan you hold and Remote Control on terms that permit your use, keeps your plan eligible for Remote Control, and does not change, limit or enforce them against your account or your pattern of use;

(c) the browser you use and the store you obtained the Extension from keep the Extension available, compatible and enabled, and do not remove or disable it;

(d) you keep your own accounts, do not share them, and keep your sign-ins current;

(e) the internet connections between your browser, your institution's systems and these services work.

Licensor may also stop offering Beethoven, the Trial Edition or a version of either at any time, as section 9 says.

8. ASSUMPTION OF RISK

You choose to use Beethoven knowing section 7. You accept the risk that any Named Dependency fails or changes, that Beethoven stops working as a result, and that work you had running, files you had in a worker's session, or time you had planned may be lost or delayed. In particular, and as Known Risks named on the welcome page, above the box you tick, you accept the risk of these four events, which are specific to how Beethoven works: Anthropic changing or enforcing Remote Control eligibility; your university disabling or reconfiguring Open OnDemand's shell, files or reverse proxy; a browser store removing or disabling the Extension; and your institution disabling your account after wrong passwords, counting a password the Extension sent for you in the way section 5(b)(i) describes or a copy your browser re-sent by itself, with getting the account back taking days. You agree that such an event is not a defect in Beethoven, not a breach of this agreement by Licensor, and gives no claim against Licensor. This section is one of the terms named in the sentence you tick on the welcome page. It does not cover loss caused by Licensor's own gross negligence, wilful misconduct or fraud.

9. EVALUATION PERIOD, SUPPORT, NO FEES, AND THE FULL EDITION

(a) Evaluation period and term. The evaluation period runs from your acceptance until the earliest of: the withdrawal of your approval, including the end of an approval that was given for a limited time; and the date Licensor ends the Trial Edition, of which Licensor gives at least 30 days' notice inside Beethoven or on the support page. This agreement lasts for the evaluation period and terminates automatically if you breach it. When it ends you must stop using Beethoven and delete it, unless you have accepted the Full Edition agreement, in which case that edition's agreement governs. Sections 4 to 8 and 10 to 23, and anything else that by its nature should survive, survive.

(b) Support. The Trial Edition comes with the documentation and the support page. Licensor may help with using Beethoven as designed, at its discretion and with no response-time promise; support does not include restoring a Named Dependency.

(c) No fees, no refunds, no remedy for outages. Nothing is owed for the Trial Edition, nothing is paid, and therefore nothing is refunded. When Beethoven stops working because of a Named Dependency, or because Licensor withdraws approval, changes or ends the Trial Edition, you have no claim against Licensor; Licensor will, where practical, restore access once the dependency works again.

(d) The Full Edition. If and when Licensor offers the Full Edition, you may continue with the Trial Edition for as long as Licensor offers it, or take up the Full Edition by accepting the Beethoven Full Edition License Agreement on the welcome page. (e) Nothing in this section limits rights that consumer law gives you and does not allow you to waive, including under the Michigan Consumer Protection Act.

10. WHAT LICENSOR RECEIVES, ACCESS RECORDS AND PRIVACY

(a) The approval check. Only after you have accepted this agreement, and only once your cluster has accepted your sign-in and your account name is known, the Extension asks Licensor's access service (https://beethoven-access.openspineconsortium.workers.dev) whether that account is approved: when you first sign in to your cluster after accepting this agreement, about once a day while it is in use, and again when you open the Extension's panel after a day has passed or after a no. Each check sends, over an encrypted connection and without cookies, your account name as your cluster confirmed it, your portal's hostname, the product name, the Extension's version, the installation identifier of section 3(e) and, as any request does, the time it was made. The service answers yes or no, and for a no may say that your account is bound to another installation, that this installation is bound to another account, or that the version is too old. Licensor's service keeps one record of the checks for each account and product: the account name, the product, the portal's hostname and the version of the latest check, when the account was first and last checked, how many checks there have been, the answer of the latest check and the reason given with a no, when the answer last changed, and a salted hash of the network address of the latest check (never the address itself); it also counts each day's checks per account and per hashed address, to limit them, and deletes those counts after two days. For each approved account it also records the installation identifier the account is bound to, with the product, the version and when that installation first and last asked, and for that installation the account it is bound to; and, when a check is refused because of another installation or another account, how many times and when the first and the last time were, with the first eight characters of a one-way hash of the refused installation's identifier. When another installation asks about your account, Licensor is told by e-mail, at most once a day per account, with a link that can move your approval to that installation. The Extension keeps a yes for up to a day, and for up to seven days when the service cannot be reached, so that an outage on Licensor's side does not stop your work; it keeps a no for ten minutes.

(b) Two files. Once a day, and only after you have accepted this agreement, the Extension also fetches from Licensor's website a small file naming the address of the access service (https://openspineconsortium.com/beethoven/services.json) and a signed list of withdrawn versions (https://openspineconsortium.com/beethoven/killlist.json). Those requests are sent without cookies and carry nothing about you beyond what any web request carries (your network address). The check in (a) and these two files are the only requests the Extension makes to Licensor.

(c) The Extension sends no error reports, no crash reports and no usage data, and there is no activation step: it has no code for them and no address to send them to. Your acceptance record (the version and hash of this text, the summary and the sentence shown, what you ticked, whether you opened the full text, the time, the install id, your account name once known, the software versions), your statements, your audit log, your settings, a password you chose to save (section 5(b)(i)) and what the Extension remembers about your worker stay in your browser; Licensor does not receive them. The install id is the installation identifier of section 3(e), which the approval check in (a) sends, as it sends your account name.

(d) Access records. An access request on the request page records what you enter there: your account name, your name, your institutional e-mail, the Google account at which you are to receive the invitation to the private listing (Licensor adds it to the Google Group that may open that listing), what you will use Beethoven for and, if you attach one, your CV; and, when the service asks you to confirm your institutional mailbox, the time you confirmed it. Licensor's own records hold the approval and withdrawal decisions about your account, with the name and e-mail given and their dates, the installation your approval is bound to (section 3(e)) and the record of the approval checks described in (a). Licensor deletes a CV twelve months after deciding on the request (twelve months after the request, if no decision is made), or at once if it refuses the request or withdraws the approval, and keeps the other records for the life of your access and six years after, to prove the license and its terms.

(e) The full privacy statement is in PRIVACY.md, which forms part of this agreement.

Beethoven is a research and teaching tool. It is not a medical device and must not be used for diagnosis, treatment or any other clinical decision, or as a source of medical advice, or in any setting where its failure could cause injury, death or damage to property. Because of section 5(e), it must not be used on protected health information, FERPA-protected education records, data collected under an IRB protocol that has not approved this use, or export-controlled technical data.

17. UPDATES AND CHANGES TO THESE TERMS

Updates to the Extension are distributed through its private listing on the Chrome Web Store, and your browser installs them by itself. A Framework that an earlier version of the Extension installed in your own cluster account is never updated on its own, and the Extension no longer installs or updates one. Where your institution's lab keeps one shared copy of the Framework, the lab updates that copy, your next worker start uses it, and the Extension shows the version in use under Details. Each version ships the terms that apply to it. Licensor may change these terms for future versions. A change is never effective merely by being posted: Beethoven shows a changed agreement on its welcome page and asks you to accept it again, by the same steps, before the new version is used. A change to section 19 or 20 applies only to disputes that arise after you accept it. If you decline a changed agreement, you may keep using the version you accepted for as long as your approval and the evaluation period last, or stop using Beethoven; earlier acceptance records are kept.

18. EXPORT AND SANCTIONS

You must comply with the export-control and sanctions laws that apply to you. You represent that you are not located in, and will not use Beethoven in, a country or region subject to a comprehensive US embargo, and that you are not on a US government restricted-party list. The Extension contains cryptography only to verify signatures (the list of withdrawn versions of section 3(d)) and, if you choose to save your cluster password (section 5(b)(i)), to encrypt it under a key your passkey releases, with your browser's own cryptography; the Framework generates random per-job tokens and, in the one-time step of section 5(b)(i), has the cluster's own ssh-keygen make a key in your account.

19. DISPUTES: NOTICE FIRST, THEN INDIVIDUAL CLAIMS IN MICHIGAN COURTS

Please read this section; it affects how disputes between you and Licensor are resolved and is one of the terms named in the sentence you tick on the welcome page.

(a) Notice and 60 days to fix it, before any lawsuit. Before starting any lawsuit or other proceeding, the party with a claim sends the other a written notice, signed by that party personally, stating their name, the e-mail in the access record, the install id shown with the acceptance record on Beethoven's settings page, what the problem is and what outcome they want. Notice to Licensor goes to the notice address on the support page at https://openspineconsortium.com/beethoven/support.html; notice to you goes to the e-mail in your access record. The parties then have 60 days to resolve it in good faith, including one telephone or video call if either asks. Completing this paragraph is a condition of bringing any claim other than in small-claims court; a court may decide, at either party's request, whether it was completed. Any time limit that applies to the claim, including (e), is paused from the day the notice is sent until the 60 days end. Licensor owes you the same notice and the same 60 days.

(b) Where. Any lawsuit or proceeding arising out of or relating to Beethoven, your access or this agreement is brought only in the state courts sitting in Wayne County, Michigan, or the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan, and both parties consent to their jurisdiction, except that (1) either party may bring an individual claim that qualifies in the small-claims court of the county where you live, and (2) you may bring a claim where you live where the law of your state gives you that right and does not allow it to be waived.

(c) CLASS-ACTION WAIVER. YOU AND LICENSOR EACH AGREE TO BRING CLAIMS AGAINST THE OTHER ONLY IN AN INDIVIDUAL CAPACITY, AND NOT AS A PLAINTIFF OR CLASS MEMBER IN ANY PURPORTED CLASS, COLLECTIVE, CONSOLIDATED OR REPRESENTATIVE PROCEEDING. Every individual remedy the law gives you remains available to you individually. If a court holds this paragraph unenforceable for a particular claim, it is severed for that claim only and the rest of this agreement stands.

(d) Fees. Each party pays its own lawyers, except that in a proceeding other than small claims the court may award the prevailing party its reasonable attorney fees and costs; this does not displace any award a statute gives you.

(e) One year to bring contract and warranty claims. Any claim for breach of this agreement, or for breach of warranty, must be brought within one year after it arose, or it is barred; the period is paused as (a) says. This paragraph does not apply to claims under a consumer-protection statute or to any claim whose period the law does not allow to be shortened.
